input: Learn to make sourdough croissants from scratch

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Sourdough croissants involve two distinct skills: maintaining a sourdough starter and laminating dough. Knowing whether the user already has an active starter changes where the plan begins.
Sourdough croissants require long cold-fermentation windows across multiple days. Knowing the user's available time per session and total timeline determines how the schedule is structured.
Kitchen equipment (stand mixer, rolling pin, bench scraper, refrigerator space, oven type) directly affects which techniques and steps are feasible.
Whether this is purely for personal skill-building or to serve others (family, guests, a small business) changes the target batch size and consistency requirements.
The user's definition of success — a technically perfect laminated crumb vs. simply edible homemade croissants — determines how rigorous the learning path needs to be.
Some learners prefer video tutorials, others prefer written recipes with diagrams or hands-on trial-and-error. The preferred learning style shapes which resources to recommend.
Knowing the user's current baking experience level (total beginner, comfortable baker, or experienced with laminated doughs) determines how much foundational detail to include in the plan.

gold.taskTitle: Learn to make sourdough croissants from scratch
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to learn how to make sourdough croissants entirely from scratch, combining sourdough fermentation with classic laminated dough technique.

questions.title: Do you already have an active sourdough starter?
questions.description: Determines whether the plan starts with building and maintaining a starter from scratch or jumps straight to the croissant dough process.

questions.title: How many days can you dedicate to one baking attempt?
questions.description: Sourdough croissants typically span 2-4 days due to fermentation and cold resting. Knowing the user's available time window shapes how the schedule is broken up.

questions.title: What key equipment do you have in your kitchen?
questions.description: Identifies whether the user has a stand mixer, enough fridge shelf space for a large flat dough, a reliable oven, and basic pastry tools — all of which affect technique choices.

questions.title: Are you baking for yourself or for others?
questions.description: Clarifies whether batch size, consistency, and presentation need to be scaled up or held to a higher standard, such as for guests or a small side business.

questions.title: What does a successful result look like to you?
questions.description: Distinguishes between a loosely defined goal (tasty homemade croissants) and a technically precise one (honeycomb crumb, distinct layers, strong sourdough tang), which calibrates the depth of the plan.

questions.title: Do you prefer video guides, written recipes, or trial-and-error?
questions.description: Determines which types of learning resources — YouTube channels, detailed written recipes, baking books, or structured experiments — to prioritise in the plan.

questions.title: How would you describe your current baking experience level?
questions.description: Knowing whether the user is a total beginner, a confident home baker, or someone already familiar with laminated doughs sets the right starting point and level of technical detail.
